Plain-text copy of the PowerShell script used to regenerate the PEP forest plot, funnel plot, pooled estimate, and supporting CSV outputs. Figures and tables Figure 1. PRISMA 2020 flow diagram showing the selection process of eligible studies. A total of 1093 records were identified from four databases (PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library), and 65 sources were included in the qualitative synthesis. Figure 2. Forest plot of PEP incidence after pediatric ERCP. Random-effects meta-analysis of logittransformed proportions across 15 non-overlapping primary studies with extractable PEP numerators and denominators. The pooled PEP incidence was 7.3% (95% CI, 5.1% to 10.4%; I-squared = 83.7%). Denominators follow the reporting unit used in each source, and source-level verification notes are provided in the extraction dataset. Figure 2. Forest plot of PEP incidence after pediatric ERCP Figure 3. Evidence map of risk domains for post-ERCP complications in children. This figure compares patient-related and procedure-related risk domains reported across four major post-ERCP complication categories. Procedure-related factors, particularly pancreatic duct manipulation and sphincterotomy, accounted for most recurring risk signals, whereas patient-level factors, including younger age and prior pancreatitis, also contributed to risk. This bar graph illustrates the estimated incidence of PEP across pediatric age groups and should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating rather than definitive. Figure 5. Reported effect estimates for selected PEP risk factors in children. Reported odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals are shown for key predictors where extractable estimates were available. Because covariate adjustment varied across source studies, this visual summary is descriptive rather than a pooled predictor meta-analysis. ARTICLE IN PRESS Younger age History of pancreatitis Pancreatic duct cannulation Descriptive evidence map based on extractable reported estimates; not a de novo pooled meta-analysis. Figure 6. Summary of prevention strategies for PEP in children. This horizontal bar chart summarizes prophylactic approaches according to clinical utility and maturity of supporting evidence. Experienced operator involvement and minimized pancreatic manipulation received the highest recommendation levels, whereas rectal NSAIDs and intravenous hydration still require stronger pediatric validation. Figure 7. Pragmatic severity and management framework for PEP in children. A simplified framework for PEP severity and stepwise management in children, adapted from revised Atlanta concepts and pediatric practice considerations. It should be used as a practical clinical framework rather than a validated pediatric severity score. ARTICLE IN PRESS Mild Clinical signals - Pain and enzyme rise - No organ failure - No local complication Care focus - Fluids and analgesia Adapted from adult Atlanta concepts; pediatric-specific validation remains limited. Use as a pragmatic escalation framework, not as a validated pediatric severity score. Figure 8. Funnel plot for PEP incidence after pediatric ERCP. Exploratory funnel plot based on logittransformed PEP proportions from studies included in Figure 2. The plot screens for small-study effects and should be interpreted cautiously because of substantial heterogeneity, rare-event behavior, and mixed patient/procedure denominators. Figure 8. top_evidence.text: This systematic review and meta-analysis was reported in accordance with PRISMA 2020[15]. The protocol was prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251084264), in accordance with best practice guidelines to ensure transparent reporting and reduce reporting bias.

top_evidence.text: Data extraction was independently conducted by two reviewers using a standardized form. Any discrepancies were resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer. For each primary study, we collected first author, year, country, study design, sample size, number of ERCP procedures, mean or median age, ERCP indications, procedure type, follow-up duration, adverse-event definitions or reporting windows, event numerators and denominators for PEP, bleeding, perforation, cholangitis or infection, severity classification, risk factors, and management strategies. For PEP, we recorded whether the denominator represented ERCP procedures, patients, first ERCP per child, or a mixed/unclear reporting unit. We retained the denominator unit used by the source rather than converting procedure-level data to patient-level data when repeat procedures per child were not consistently reported. For prior systematic reviews and meta-analyses, we extracted scope, search period, included study types, pooled estimates, and overlap with primary studies to avoid

top_evidence.document_title: Post-ERCP adverse events in children: a systematic review and meta-analysis of postERCP pancreatitis incidence with synthesis of risk factors and prevention strategies
top_evidence.text: Meta-analysis was conducted only for outcomes reported by at least three non-overlapping primary studies with extractable numerators and denominators. Pooled incidences were estimated using random-effects models for proportions, with variance stabilization for rare events where appropriate. Results were expressed as pooled proportions with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Between-study heterogeneity was assessed using Cochran Q and the I-squared statistic. Heterogeneity was interpreted as low, moderate, substantial, or considerable using conventional thresholds, while acknowledging that I-squared may be unstable in rare-event analyses. We prespecified subgroup exploration by age group, ERCP indication, procedure type, pancreatic duct manipulation or contrast injection, sphincterotomy, and operator or center volume. Formal subgroup meta-analysis was not forced when studies did not provide stratified PEP event counts, because doing so would have required ecological assumptions. These variables were therefore summarized as explanatory domains for heterogeneity and risk. Sensitivity analyses were planned by excluding studies at high risk of bias, studies with unclear adverseevent definitions, and studies with potential cohort overlap. In response to peer review, we also added a post hoc denominator-unit sensitivity summary, separating procedure-level studies from patient-level or first-ERCP-perchild studies and retaining a mixed/unclear category when the source did not permit classification. Risk-factor effect estimates were not pooled when exposure definitions, covariate adjustment, or reporting units differed substantially. These data were summarized narratively and, where appropriate, displayed as reported estimates. ARTICLE IN PRESS Publication bias was assessed visually using funnel plots and statistically using Egger test only for outcomes with at least ten eligible studies. Funnel plots were not generated for rare outcomes with fewer than ten studies because asymmetry tests would be unreliable. All tests were two-sided. For analyses other than Cochran's Q test for heterogeneity, P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. For Cochran's Q test, P < 0.10 was considered indicative of potential between-study heterogeneity because this test has limited power when relatively few studies are included. Heterogeneity was interpreted together with I² and τ². AI-assisted tools were used during revision for language editing and formatting checks. The authors verified the data extraction, statistical analyses, interpretation, and final text and take full responsibility for the manuscript.

top_evidence.text: This systematic review included 65 sources in the qualitative synthesis, consisting primarily of contemporary pediatric ERCP primary studies and selected prior systematic reviews or meta-analyses used for contextual benchmarking[2-14, 19-71]. Prior reviews were not treated as independent primary data and their pooled estimates were not combined with overlapping primary studies. A detailed account of the literature screening and selection process, following PRISMA 2020 principles, is illustrated in Figure 1.
